passage: Nirmala, you said you can't do spreadsheet formulas. Let me tell you about me at twenty-five, at the post office in Amritsar, the year the computers came. Everyone younger learned fast. I sat there resenting the machine, saying, "I can't do this. I'm not a computer person." One evening the postmaster, an old Sikh gentleman, heard me and said, "Gurpreet, you can't do it yet. What will you try next?" That word annoyed me, honestly. But I went home and wrote on a paper: "Can't do it YET. Next: ask Harjit to show me the entry screen, practise ten entries a day." It wasn't magic. My first method, copying from the manual, didn't help at all. Harjit's way did. So, Nirmala: yet, and then, what will you try?

qa.q: What did young Gurpreet write on the paper at home?
qa.a: "Can't do it YET. Next: ask Harjit to show me the entry screen, practise ten entries a day."

qa.q: Why did the word "yet" annoy young Gurpreet at first?
qa.a: Gurpreet was full of resentment toward the machine and felt stuck; "yet" sounded too easy, as if it brushed aside how hard it felt.

qa.q: Which choice made "yet" actually work for Gurpreet?
qa.a: Pairing it with a concrete next step, and switching from the manual to Harjit's way when the first method failed.

qa.q: What might Nirmala take from this story?
qa.a: Nirmala may see that struggling with formulas now doesn't close the future, and that the useful question is what to try next.

grounding: An elder recalls turning 'I can't' into 'I can't yet' at twenty-five and pairing it with a better strategy.

passage: Maria had failed her driving test in Panaji twice, both times on the slope start, and her new job at a clinic in Mapusa needed her driving in three weeks. The monsoon had turned the practice ground to mud. After the second fail she sat in Simran's car in the rain and said, "I can't do this. I'm just not a driver." Simran didn't argue. "You can't do slope starts yet. What haven't you tried?" Maria wiped her eyes, annoyed. Then she thought. She had only ever practised on flat roads. She'd never used the handbrake method the instructor mentioned. The next morning, rain still falling, she found a quiet sloping lane near the church and did twenty slope starts with the handbrake. Nineteen didn't roll back.

qa.q: How many of Maria's slope starts didn't roll back?
qa.a: Nineteen of twenty.

qa.q: Why was Maria annoyed when Simran said "yet"?
qa.a: After two fails and with a deadline looming, she felt defeated, and "yet" seemed to brush past how bad she felt.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what choice followed?
qa.a: Simran's question about what she hadn't tried; Maria chose to practise on a real slope with the handbrake method instead of flat roads.

qa.q: How might Simran feel seeing Maria practise in the rain?
qa.a: Simran may feel glad that a short question helped, and quietly proud of a friend who turned tears into a plan.

grounding: An adult under time pressure reframes 'I can't drive' as 'not yet' and finds a better practice strategy.

passage: At the Nariman Point office, Hrithik's first client presentation had gone badly: he lost his place, read from the slides, and watched the client check his phone. Back at his desk he muttered, "I can't present. Some people just can't." Pankaj, the senior manager, overheard. "You can't present yet," Pankaj said. "So what's the next thing to try?" Hrithik almost rolled his eyes; it sounded like a poster. But that night he wrote two lines: "Can't present yet. Try: practise out loud three times, use cue cards not slides." He rehearsed in the empty conference room, twice to the wall and once to Pankaj. The next presentation wasn't perfect. But he didn't read from the slides, and the client asked two questions.

qa.q: What did Hrithik decide to use instead of reading from the slides?
qa.a: Cue cards.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik almost roll his eyes at Pankaj's "yet"?
qa.a: Still stinging from the bad presentation, he felt it was a slogan that ignored how badly things had gone.

qa.q: Which choice turned "yet" into progress?
qa.a: Writing a concrete plan, practising aloud and using cue cards, so the word led to a better strategy rather than just hope.

qa.q: How might Pankaj see Hrithik's second presentation?
qa.a: Pankaj would likely see real progress, fewer slides read aloud and a client asking questions, and feel the nudge was worth it.

grounding: An adult reframes a failed presentation with 'not yet' and a specific practice plan, and improves.

passage:
"I can't do it, Saurabh. I'm quitting the swimming class."
Her husband looked up from the laptop. "What happened?"
"Everyone else floated by week three. I still sink like a stone. I'm twenty-five, I'm too old, I just can't swim."
"Can't, or can't yet?"
Sonali threw a wet towel at him. "Don't do the poster thing."
"I'm not. Just... what have you tried?"
She sat down, dripping. "Kicking harder. It makes it worse."
"So kicking harder isn't it. What else is there?"
A pause. "The coach said something about breathing out slowly and keeping my head down. I kept lifting it to look."
"So try that on Saturday?"
"Fine." She wrung out her hair. "I can't float. Yet." She said the last word as if she didn't quite trust it. "And I'll ask the coach to watch my head."

qa.q: What did the coach say about breathing and her head?
qa.a: Breathing out slowly and keeping her head down.

qa.q: What is Sonali feeling when she says 'Yet' as if she doesn't quite trust it?
qa.a: Still frustrated and doubtful, but opening a door; she half-believes progress is possible and is willing to test it.

qa.q: What turning point in the conversation helped Sonali plan her next try?
qa.a: Saurabh asking what she had tried; seeing that kicking harder made it worse led her to a new strategy, breathing out and head down, with the coach watching.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel when the towel comes flying?
qa.a: Saurabh probably takes it with good humour 😄, understands her frustration, and chooses questions over slogans so she doesn't feel lectured.

grounding: An adult turns 'I can't swim' into 'I can't yet' and pairs it with a new strategy to try next.

passage: When I moved to Bengaluru for my first nursing job, I told everyone, "I can't speak Kannada. I'm hopeless with languages." I'm Beena, from Kottayam. For three months I pointed and smiled at patients' families and felt useless. My friend Kiranjit, a Punjabi who'd learned Tamil in Chennai, said, "You mean you can't yet." I rolled my eyes. But the word stuck. Then she asked, "What have you actually tried?" Honestly, just a phrasebook I never opened. So I changed the plan: five ward phrases a week, written on my palm, used with real patients, and the night-shift attendant correcting me. Four months later I can explain the meal times and ask where it hurts. Plenty still goes over my head. But "I can't" has become "not yet, and here are next week's five."

qa.q: How many ward phrases did Beena learn each week?
qa.a: Five ward phrases a week.

qa.q: Why did Beena feel useless in the first three months?
qa.a: Without Kannada, Beena could only point and smile instead of really helping families, and 'I'm hopeless with languages' made the gap feel permanent.

qa.q: What choice turned 'yet' into real progress for Beena?
qa.a: Swapping the unopened phrasebook for five phrases a week, used on the ward and corrected by the night-shift attendant; the word opened the door and the method did the work.

qa.q: How might patients' families experience the change in Beena?
qa.a: They can now hear the meal times and be asked where it hurts in their own language, which likely makes them feel more cared for and less anxious.

grounding: An adult replaces 'I can't speak the language' with 'not yet' and backs it with a concrete weekly method.
